title: Senior's toolkit: running and exploring Python
summary: The commands and habits for running scripts, poking at values and reading docs without leaving the terminal.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: running and exploring Python
steps.body: Experienced Python developers try things in seconds: a one-liner, a REPL, a quick debug print. These are the commands they type without thinking.

toolkit.what: Run one line of code without making a file. Good for checking a version, a module or a quick calculation.
flags: run a module as a program (`python -m venv`, `python -m pytest`)

toolkit.what: Run a script, then stay in the REPL with all its variables. If the script crashes, you land at the prompt with the state it had.
flags: interactive after the script ends or crashes
toolkit.when: a script printed something odd and you want to look at its variables

toolkit.what: Read the docs and list the attributes of anything, right in the REPL. Faster than a web search for "what does split take?".
flags: the actual type of a value

toolkit.what: The self-documenting f-string: prints the expression, an `=` and its value. The quickest honest debug print.
Run a script inside the project's environment, installing what it needs first. No activating, no "wrong Python".
flags: add a package just for this run

toolkit.what: On Windows, the `py` launcher lists every installed Python and starts a specific one.
flags: list installed versions with their paths
toolkit.when: "it works on my machine" and you suspect two Pythons

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it is for.
pairs: run one line without a file
keep the variables after the script ends
run an installed module as a program
add a package for this run only
read a function's docs in the REPL

steps.explain: `{x=}` prints the expression text, `=`, then `repr()` of the value, so strings inside the list keep their quotes. A format spec after the `=` formats the value.

steps.prompt: You ran `uv add rich` in your project, and it worked. Now `python receipt.py` fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rich'`. What is the likely cause?
options: `python` is the system Python, not the project's `.venv`; run `uv run receipt.py` instead
`rich` must also be installed with `pip install rich --global`
The file must be renamed to `rich.py`
`uv add` only downloads the package; you must restart the computer
steps.explain: `uv add` installs into the project's `.venv`. A bare `python` may be another interpreter. `uv run` always uses the project's environment, and `python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"` shows which Python you actually ran.

steps.prompt: Print the running Python's version from the terminal without creating a file.
steps.explain: `-c` runs the quoted code. `sys.version` is the full version string; `sys.executable` would tell you which interpreter it is.

steps.prompt: Which do you reach for first?
items: Look at the variables a script left behind after it crashed
Try a few calls on the data a script just loaded
List the methods a `Path` object has
Log a value together with its name in one quick line
Print `price` and `qty` without typing their names twice

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When you are unsure what a function does, ask the REPL (`help`, `dir`, a quick `python -c`) before you search the web. Run project code with `uv run` so you always get the right interpreter, and use `f"{x=}"` for throwaway debug prints, then delete them before you commit.
